questions.q: Why does `bid()` check `if (highestBidder != address(0))` before adding to bids?
options: Because on the very first bid, there's no previous bidder yet to refund
To prevent any bids from ever being placed
Because address(0) is the seller's real address
It has no real purpose and could be removed safely
questions.explain: address(0) is the default, unset value for highestBidder — this guard avoids crediting a refund to a bidder that doesn't actually exist yet.

questions.q: What real vulnerability does resetting `bids[msg.sender] = 0` before sending ETH actually prevent?
options: A reentrancy attack, where a malicious contract could call withdraw again before the first call finishes
An integer overflow in the balance
A transaction running out of gas
The auction ending too early
questions.explain: If the balance were reset after sending ETH, a malicious receiving contract could re-enter withdraw before the first call completes, draining funds repeatedly.

questions.q: What is the real, named pattern this lesson demonstrates for writing safe withdrawal functions?
options: Checks-effects-interactions — update your own state before making any external call
Interactions-effects-checks
There is no real named pattern for this
Always perform the external call first, then update state
questions.explain: The checks-effects-interactions pattern is the real, standard Solidity security practice: verify conditions, update your own state, and only then interact with external addresses or send funds.

questions.q: Why is `end()` deliberately left callable by anyone, rather than restricted to the seller?
options: So a seller who never calls it doesn't permanently lock everyone else's funds in the contract
Because restricting it to the seller would make the contract cheaper to run
Because only the seller is technically capable of calling any function
There's no real reason — it was an oversight
questions.explain: If only the seller could call end(), an unresponsive seller could leave the highest bidder's NFT and everyone's ETH stuck in the contract indefinitely.

questions.q: What would actually go wrong if `withdraw` sent ETH before resetting `bids[msg.sender]` to zero?
options: A malicious contract could re-enter withdraw while its balance was still non-zero, draining funds multiple times
The function would simply fail to compile
It would cost slightly more gas but behave identically otherwise
Nothing — the order of these two lines doesn't actually matter
questions.explain: This is the exact real reentrancy vulnerability the lesson warns about — swapping the order lets an attacker call withdraw again before their balance is actually zeroed.
